cards.source_title: Prompting vs JSON Mode vs Function Calling vs Constrained Generation vs SAP
cards.source_date: 2024-07-29 (day from blog index; year inferred, page shows only 'over 2 years ago')
cards.quote: The key idea behind SAP is to assume that the model will make mistakes
cards.claim: A lenient, schema-aware parser that repairs free-text output by minimum edits beats native function calling. The post rates LLM-retry repair 1 of 5 because it 'adds unbounded latency and costs'.
cards.evidence: BFCL, n=1000 per model, run by SAP's own authors who disclose bias. Accuracy % as function calling / Python AST parser / SAP: gpt-3.5-turbo 87.5/75.8/92; gpt-4o 87.4/82.1/93; claude-3-haiku 57.3/82.6/91.7; gpt-4o-mini 19.8/51.8/92.4; claude-3-5-sonnet 78.1/93.8/94.4. Llama-3.1 8B row has no function-calling value. Metric, prompts and the function-calling configuration are not stated. All 2024-era models.
cards.first_guess: Our forced StructuredOutput path is validate-then-retry, the pattern the post rates worst. The transferable part is script-side coercion of near-miss values (single string to array, enum case-folding) before rejecting. Low priority until a contract shows real retry cost.

cards.source_title: Beating OpenAI's structured outputs on cost, accuracy and speed — An interactive deep-dive
cards.source_date: 2024-08-13 (day from blog index; year inferred, page shows 'about 2 years ago')
cards.quote: It's easily 2-4x faster than OpenAI's FC-strict API.
cards.claim: Prompt plus type definitions plus SAP is cheaper, more accurate and 2-4x faster than OpenAI strict function calling on BFCL. gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o-mini and claude-haiku with BAML land within 2% of gpt-4o with structured output. FC-strict made gpt-4o-2024-08-06 worse than naive function calling.
cards.evidence: Only two figures are readable in prose: '2-4x faster' (against FC-strict) and 'less than 2%'. No cost figures, no n, no BFCL version; subsets named simple, parallel, multiple. Per-model scores are in an interactive chart that did not render. Footnotes: 100% is unreachable because some BFCL prompts and assertions are ambiguous, and the authors did not fix the assertions, to stay comparable with earlier runs.
cards.first_guess: Do not cite as evidence about current Claude models; every model tested is 2024-era. The reusable lesson is that a test suite with unsatisfiable assertions has a hidden ceiling, so any brief test we write should first check that each assertion can be met (see B-13).

cards.source_date: 2025-12-14 (blog index; the post carries an update dated Dec 21)
cards.quote: structured outputs create false confidence: it's entirely non-obvious that you're sacrificing output quality
cards.claim: A forced schema removes the model's ability to refuse, warn or explain, and can lower extraction quality while hiding it. Error branches in the schema cannot be enumerated in advance. The post's alternative is a free-form answer plus a tolerant parser, which it also calls a defense-in-depth layer against prompt injection.
cards.evidence: One receipt test on gpt-5.2-2025-12-11: banana quantity 1 with structured outputs versus the correct 0.46 free-form. Two other test images (an elephant, a currency-exchange receipt) are described but no results are reported. Older BFCL figure with gpt-4o: 93.63% prompt-and-parse versus 91.37% constrained decoding, which the author says should be re-run. The post's own clarifications call the 'Let Me Speak Freely' paper flawed.
cards.first_guess: Every agent in our harness is schema-forced. Keep an always-present free-text 'notes' field plus an honest-empty escape (tool_status, could_not_read) in each contract, and let skeptic briefs return 'cannot judge'. Do not drop forced schemas on this evidence (see B-04).

cards.source_title: Structured outputs create false confidence (Hacker News thread, 155 points, 66 comments)
cards.quote: This is unfair and biases the results towards what they wanted to show.
cards.claim: The community judged B-03's evidence confounded: free-form chain-of-thought plus JSON compared with non-CoT structured output. The banana case was arguably correct given an 'assume 1' instruction. Practitioner takeaways: schema field order matters (reasoning placed after the answer lets the model answer first), a two-pass extract-then-structure approach works, and reasoning models with hidden thinking avoid the trade-off.
cards.evidence: Quote is from commenter dcastm. Simon Willison asked for a more extensive formal eval. Commenter reports: 99.7% field accuracy on receipts with free-form extraction then a structured pass; no significant difference in another commenter's RAG pipeline. Commenters point to dottxt/Outlines posts showing constrained decoding helps. No head-to-head study was produced by anyone; reports are unverified.
cards.first_guess: One cheap check: in every contract, put reasoning and evidence properties before verdict and severity properties, since property order is generation order. Also apply the thread's lesson to ourselves: when comparing two brief versions, change only the variable under test.

cards.source_title: Your prompts are using 4x more tokens than you need
cards.quote: Type-definitions use 60% less tokens than JSON schemas, with no loss of information.
cards.claim: Rendering the output schema as TypeScript-like type definitions instead of generated JSON Schema cuts schema tokens and did not hurt extraction quality. On a small model it removed schema-echo failures.
cards.evidence: Schema portion only, Instructor-generated JSON Schema: OrderInfo 56 tokens versus 14 (4x); a complex nested example about 66% fewer; the 4x and 60% figures come from different examples, not one benchmark. Llama 2 7B, 100 tests: 6% failure with JSON Schema (it echoed schema structures) versus 0% with type definitions. One model, one task. The mechanism explanations are the author's speculation. Test code is in the baml-pydantic-comparison repo (not opened). The v0 docs page restates it as about 180 versus 35 tokens (80%).
cards.first_guess: We do not control how the Workflow tool renders our schema into the forced tool. The only lever is schema size (short enums, few optional fields, terse descriptions). At most a schema-size budget, nothing to adopt.

cards.source_title: LLMs do not understand numbers (with the companion post 'Beware When Using TOON')
cards.quote: Stop writing prompts assuming that LLMs understand numbers:
cards.claim: Do not ask a model for a confidence score, a sum of receipt items, or a row count. The TOON post applies the same point: TOON needs array lengths written out, so the model has to count, and BAML therefore accepts TOON as input but declines it as output.
cards.evidence: One informal test on gpt-5.1: asked to count functions, types and imports in a large snippet, it first declined, then returned fn_count 82 with a 68-element list, type_count 8 with 8 names, import_count 54 with 55 names. No benchmark, no token or accuracy figures in either post; the TOON post gives no JSON-versus-TOON cost comparison.
cards.first_guess: Audit our contracts for model-asserted counts, scores and confidences. Let the script compute counts from array lengths and keep verdict, severity and evidence_kind as enums (the existing evidence_kind enum already fits). For the knowledge-store CLI, TOON-style compact formats are not a free lunch; plain output stays.

cards.source_title: Software Factories Still Need Human Operators: Building 6 BAML SDKs for 6 Programming Languages in 1 Week
cards.quote: skilled human operators, who know how to push their coding agents to their limits
cards.claim: Six SDK bridges in a week by six engineers worked only after about 2 months of human architecture, about 1 day of hand-written reference docs, shared test infrastructure and CI on three operating systems. Listing test cases is insufficient to steer an agent to the correct recursive implementation, and agent-written docs missed the complex recursive cases.
cards.evidence: One project, self-reported: 6 bridges, 6 engineers x 6 days, 8 supported host languages. No model or agent product named, no defect or rework rates, nothing on orchestration. The recursive-callback example (second-order callbacks failing after first-order ones passed) is the only concrete failure.
cards.first_guess: Supports hand-written reference briefs plus a 'state of completeness' doc per phase, and warns that example-based tests give false coverage for compositional behaviour. Lands in review briefs and the ship plan's gates, not in the five areas.

cards.source_title: Using UUIDs in prompts is bad
cards.source_date: 2025-10-03 (date from the page's asset path; page shows 'about 1 year ago')
cards.quote: Each UUID costs a whopping 24 tokens
cards.claim: Replace UUIDs with small integers before the call and map them back afterwards. This cuts tokens and sharply cuts echo and aggregation errors. The author advises benchmarking your own use case.
cards.evidence: 200 items across 100 class IDs on Claude Haiku, two runs per arm: raw UUIDs 29 and 68 errors (avg 48.5), integer IDs 7 and 5 (avg 6), UUID-to-int remap 5 and 6 (avg 5.5). Smaller test of 100 items and 50 classes: all arms made 2-4 errors. Opus 4: 100% accuracy with integer IDs versus 80% with UUIDs. Task was aggregation, chosen because it is auto-verifiable. Two runs per arm, one task type.
cards.first_guess: When a script hands records to an agent (verifier inputs, knowledge-store rows), give short handles such as B-01 or KS-O7 and map back in code. Never make an agent echo a UUID, long hash or full SHA. Our card ids are already short; check wherever an agent must repeat a commit or content hash.

cards.source_date: 2025-10-10 to 2025-11-05 incident (year inferred; blog index lists Nov 14, page shows '12 months ago')
cards.quote: it's famously easy for the eyes to glaze over when reading a vibe-coded PR.
cards.claim: BAML 0.212.0 shipped accidental 30-second default timeouts that returned empty payloads, fixed in 0.213.0. Cause was 4 or 5 stacked risk factors: two vibe-coded implementations, docs written for the unmerged one, swallowed errors, and an untested combination. Fix: enumerate the dimensions (3 timeout types x 2 modes = 6 combinations) and sample the whole matrix; budget stacked risk; give risky work one end-to-end owner.
cards.evidence: A single dated post-mortem by the maintainers: Oct 10 start, Oct 28 deploy of 0.212.0, Nov 05 report and same-day 0.213.0; the untested path was request_timeout_ms on streaming requests. Dates carry no year on the page.
cards.first_guess: Add two lines to Opus review briefs: 'list the dimensions of this change and show which combinations the tests cover' and 'which implementation do the docs describe?'. Process idea for review gates, outside the five areas.

cards.source_title: Announcing LLM Eval Support for Python, Ruby, Typescript, Go, and more.
cards.quote: fail the test if the LLM output doesn't match the expected output
cards.claim: A test block supplies arguments to a typed prompt function. @@assert fails the test; @@check records a named boolean beside the result (Launch Week Day 3 states the same split for @assert and @check). Expressions can read the result, earlier checks and latency_ms. Tests need only BAML, not the host language. LLM-as-judge was not supported.
cards.evidence: Feature announcement with no numbers or benchmarks. Now stale: BAML 0.18.0 removed the v0 test-block syntax, and v1 tests are expression bodies such as test 'name' { assert.equal(a, b) }. The later AI That Works notes describe repeated runs and relative gates instead (B-13).
cards.first_guess: A brief regression test needs no BAML: one fixed input plus a plain JS function over the returned object. Assert (throw) that the quote is at most 15 words, evidence strings match 'path:line — quote', ids are unique and the count is at most 15. Check (record, do not reject) softer properties. Deterministic checks only, no model judgement.

cards.source_title: BAML (product homepage) with HN launch thread 'Baml: The Programming Language for Agents'
cards.quote: BAML is a Turing-complete programming language designed for software written by agents and humans.
cards.claim: The prior assessment is out of date. BAML is now a Turing-complete language for agent-written software, 'currently pre-1.0'. The typed-LLM-function DSL is legacy v0, and the docs 'Why BAML' page says v1 is a separate language. Releases since 0.17 (Aug 2026) each carry long breaking-change lists: v0 test blocks and Jinja dropped (0.18.0), many env-var, SDK-option and timeout renames (0.21.0), shipped as canary builds.
cards.evidence: First-party homepage and release notes; the homepage states 'some APIs and tooling may continue to evolve'. HN thread (8 points, 5 comments): an author says agents 'saved 30% tokens navigating baml codebases vs TypeScript ones', with no method; one commenter objects to the 'for agents' framing. Homepage lists 'Native LLM functions, tests, testsets, and evaluations' as built in.
cards.first_guess: Corrects the idea that BAML is a stable prompt-function DSL we could adopt for contracts. It is useful only as a design reference. Any adoption would pin a toolchain on a pre-1.0 language whose syntax breaks about every release, and needs an owner decision; nothing to install.

cards.quote: `baml query` lets you inspect recordings without adding application logging.
cards.claim: v1 records every run (spans, provider HTTP request and response bodies, usage and cost) and exposes it through SQL over four relations. Per-call trace options control what is captured, and retry and fallback attempts appear as their own spans. Cost is accumulated as integer nanodollars, taken from captured provider responses.
cards.evidence: Release notes only, no measurements. The post warns that 'HTTP bodies participate in recordings', so telemetry policy must be chosen deliberately for sensitive requests. Cloud recording goes through Boundary's hosted endpoint (opt-in login).
cards.first_guess: Reusable idea is record-by-default: each agent() call could emit {brief hash, schema hash, model, output, usage} so a brief edit can be diffed against earlier outputs. Workflow scripts have no filesystem, so records would have to travel in the returned object to the main session. Needs an owner decision; redact bodies deliberately.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #67: Your Model is Already Obsolete
cards.quote: You need it to be no worse.
cards.claim: Treat a model swap as a regression test, not a quality contest. Run a case corpus, converted to BAML test blocks, against incumbent and candidates, reporting accuracy, token cost and p95 latency. Gate relatively (candidate no worse than incumbent), run three repeats per case by default, review only the cases where candidate and incumbent disagree, and refuse to judge when an input such as price is unverified.
cards.evidence: One worked example with gpt-4o as incumbent and claude-sonnet-5 and gemini-3.6-flash as candidates; p50 latency 1293 ms, 2523 ms and 4605 ms respectively. Failure lessons stated: defaulting a missing price to 0.0 let unpriced models pass the cost gate, and one unsatisfiable assertion made the optimizer chase 'a test no output could satisfy'. Corpus size not seen.
cards.first_guess: Closest fit to area (b). To compare a revised brief with the current one: fixed case set, three repeats, relative gate, owner sees only disagreements, and a missing fixture or cost blocks scoring instead of defaulting. Buildable as a Workflow script; no BAML needed.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #54: Harness Engineering Without the Hype
cards.quote: Evals are the spec that outlives everything else.
cards.claim: A harness is the operating system around a 'while true' agent loop. Eval sets grounded in production traces outlive any harness or model. Exhaust single-loop improvements before adding a second loop or sub-agent, inspect what the agent actually returns, and treat a generated system prompt that looks like 60 if-else cases as overfit. Build your own harness only if you will train a model on your tools.
cards.evidence: Show notes of a discussion, no measurements. Figures such as a '40-50 person engineering team' behind off-the-shelf harnesses and a '5-10%' compounding edge from faster model iteration are the speakers' estimates.
cards.first_guess: Mostly confirms existing rules (judge by output, restrain sub-agents). The portable idea is a small durable golden set of inputs with expected properties per brief, so it survives model changes. Not new, but a useful naming for area (b).

cards.source_title: OpenAI Decisions is coming to BAML v1 (with the companion 'TypeSafe AI's Jev model is coming to BAML v1')
cards.quote: The return type defines what judgments to make.
cards.claim: In BAML v1 the declared return type becomes a set of closed classification questions sent to a classifier endpoint: bool and float become predicates, enums and finite unions become choices, classes become one question per leaf. float returns the raw probability for an application-chosen threshold. A confidence field is a separate independent question, not the confidence of another field. Free-form strings, ints and arrays are unsupported.
cards.evidence: Integration documentation with no benchmarks. The Jev post also reports no accuracy figures. The post advises using 'labeled examples from your application' to choose thresholds and assess classification quality.
cards.first_guess: Mirrors our closed-set verdict and severity enums. We cannot call these endpoints from Claude Code, so idea-only: if a verifier ever reports a probability, keep it a separate field and calibrate it on labelled examples. Otherwise no landing.

notes: WebFetch returns small-model answers, not raw pages; every quote was re-checked by a second fetch asking for the exact sentence, and quotes are fragments where the sentence ran long. Blog pages show only relative ages, so year-less dates are inferred and flagged. Prior assessment corrected: BAML is now a pre-1.0 agent language (v0 DSL legacy; breaking changes nearly every release). All numbers are vendor-run, on 2024-era models for SAP and BFCL. No Launch HN thread exists, only a 2024 Show HN. Nothing installed or run.
